Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

Climate finance has become one of the central topics in the global climate change discourse. Every Conference of Parties (COP) under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) discusses billions of dollars in climate finance and announces new commitments, making pledges and debating on how financial resources should be mobilized. From COP15 in Copenhagen to COP30 in Brazil, the concept of climate finance has evolved significantly, reshaping both global negotiations and expectations. The Copenhagen Accord marked a turning point by making a commitment to mobilize $100 billion annually and paving the way for the establishment of the Green Climate Fund (GCF). The Paris Agreement adopted at COP21 in 2015 further institutionalized the climate finance architecture, placing it at the centre of global efforts to support mitigation, adaptation and resilience-building in developing countries. More recently, COP29, widely described as the “finance COP,” adopted New Quantified Climate Goals (NCQG) and agreed to mobilize $300bn per year by 2035. Yet the outcome also exposed a widening gap between ambition and reality. While developing and least developed countries argued that around $5-6 trillion was required annually to meet the global climate goals, the negotiated amount stood at only $300bn. How these resources will be mobilized, delivered, and accessed remains unresolved. An uncomfortable question also remains: Has climate finance actually strengthened the resilience of countries like Bangladesh? The answer is not as straightforward as the volume of funding might suggest. Much of the climate finance debate continues to focus on how much money is committed or disbursed. Success is often measured in mobilization of millions or billions of dollars, the number of approved projects, or the volume of international funding received. While these figures are important, they reveal very little about whether climate finance is creating long-term resilience where it matters most. Although the Paris agreement didn’t mention the word “compensation,” for developed nations, climate finance is considered an obligation arising from historical responsibility for greenhouse gas emissions. For developing and least developed countries, it is a matter of climate justice, recognizing that those who have contributed the least to climate change are experiencing the worst consequences of climate change. Even when finance becomes available, accessing funds is rarely straightforward. Climate finance operates through an increasingly complex architecture involving multilateral funds, bilateral agencies, development banks, accreditation processes, fiduciary standards, environmental safeguards, and reporting requirements. While these mechanisms are designed to ensure accountability and effectiveness, they also increase transaction costs and create significant barriers, particularly for countries with limited institutional capacity. Climate finance therefore does not move directly from international commitments to the vulnerable communities. It passes through a complex pathway of institutions, governance systems, and political processes before reaching those most vulnerable to climate change. The gap between the demand and announced amount is not the only problem in the climate finance discussion. Accessing climate finance for the least developed and developing countries is also a challenge for both the capacity gap and the complex mechanism of the climate finance instruments. The Paris Agreement encourages countries to pursue low-carbon and climate-resilient development. However, for many developing countries, climate action cannot be separated from broader development priorities. Governments must simultaneously reduce poverty, create employment, expand infrastructure, strengthen health and education systems, and improve food security. A ccessing funds remains a major challenge for many countries like Bangladesh which are the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries. Bangladesh has emerged as one of the more pro-active countries in strengthening climate governance. Over the past decade, Bangladesh has established an impressive policy architecture, including the Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan, the National Adaptation Plan, a nd the Delta Plan 2100. Climate considerations are increasingly integrated into national planning and budgeting systems, while institutions responsible for climate governance have continued to evolve. However, Bangladesh continues to seek enormous investment requirements for climate adaptation, resilient infrastructure, disaster risk reduction, renewable energy, urban development, and climate-induced displacement. These investments are essential not only for responding to climate change but also for boosting economic growth and improving living standards. The challenge is therefore much broader than accessing climate finance. Bangladesh is expected to achieve low-carbon development while continuing its journey towards upper-middle-income status. It must invest in clean energy while ensuring affordable electricity for industries and households. It must strengthen climate resilience while expanding infrastructure. It must reduce emissions while creating employment for a growing population. It must support climate adaptation while financing education, healthcare, social protection. and urban services. In other words, Bangladesh is expected to pursue climate resilience and economic prosperity simultaneously. The difficulty lies in the fact that the current climate finance architecture has not yet evolved to adequately support this bi-fold ambition. Low carbon and climate-resilient development cannot be purchased simply by increasing financial commitments. It requires institutional readiness, coherent public policy, strong local governments, effective planning and budgeting systems, private sector engagement, and long-term investment strategies. Finance remains indispensable, but finance alone cannot transform development pathways. Developing countries cannot afford to pursue climate objectives at the expense of economic development. Nor can they postpone climate action until prosperity has been achieved. The challenge is to integrate both objectives within a balanced development strategy. This requires moving beyond a project-based approach towards financing structural transformation. Climate finance should strengthen national planning systems rather than creating parallel implementation structures. It should empower local governments alongside national institutions. It should mobili z e private investment without undermining public accountability. Above all, it should recogni z e that development and climate action are mutually reinforcing rather than competing objectives. An equally important question deserves greater attention: W hat kind of financial architecture enables developing countries to simultaneously achieve prosperity, resilience, and low-carbon development? Greater financial commitments remain essential. Vulnerable countries have repeatedly argued that existing available resources are limited compared to actual requirements. However, increasing the volume of finance alone will not resolve the underlying paradox. The international community must also make climate finance more predictable, accessible, and aligned with national development priorities of the countries who are experiencing challenges of balancing economic prosperity and achieving climate goals. Funding mechanisms should reduce unnecessary complexity while strengthening country ownership. Institutional readiness should be rewarded through more flexible access to finance rather than additional procedural burdens. Most importantly, global climate finance should recogni z e that successful climate action in developing countries depends not only on reducing emissions but also on creating the economic opportunities that allow societies to thrive. The c limate f inance p aradox reminds us that expanding ambitions require equally ambitious financial and institutional reforms. Without closing the gap between expectations and implementation, developing countries will continue to face an impossible task: D elivering prosperity on a low-carbon development pathway with financial support that remains insufficient, fragmented, and difficult to access. Bangladesh’s experience shows that the challenge is not a lack of commitment. The challenge is ensuring that the global climate finance architecture evolves as rapidly as the ambitions it now seeks to achieve. Md Abul Basar is an anthropologist and governance expert, and serves as the team lea der at a Switzerland-based international organization. He can be reached at bashar.arif@gmail.com .

item.title: Treating e-waste as an opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-20

That Bangladesh generates an estimated three million metric tons of electronic waste annually, and that it recycles less than 10% of that waste through formal channels, is an extremely concerning reality for a nation that has aspirations of a more sustainable future. That the majority of our e-waste ends up in informal scrapyards, landfills, and waterways, where toxic materials contaminate the soil and air, stand in sharp contradiction to our desire for a healthier country. It is safe to say that such negligence is no longer just an environmental concern but a public health and governance crisis. The prevalence of informal recyclers dominating the sector, often working without protective gear while handling lead, mercury, cadmium, and other hazardous substances, also reflects poorly on the present state of affairs. Workers who are often below the age of 18 are frequently exposed to these toxins, with long‑term consequences for cognitive and physical development. The other component to this failure is that Bangladesh is also losing economic value. E‑waste contains recoverable materials - copper, gold, and other rare earth elements - that could support a circular economy and create jobs, with reports stating that Bangladesh could recover over $200 million in resources annually through effective recycling. Instead, these resources are being discarded or extracted unsafely, with no national system to capture their value. The solution is clear, and it starts with recognizing recycling firstly as a moral imperative but also as a means to generate value. This means investing to build a nationwide collection network and modern recycling facilities while formalizing the informal sector with training and safety standards. E‑waste is not garbage but an opportunity. Managed well, it can reduce pollution, recover valuable materials, and support our sustainable growth. Managed poorly, it will continue to be one of our most dangerous pollutants. The choice is clear.

item.title: Heat resilience must be a national priority. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-20

The World Bank’s latest findings should alarm every policy-maker in Bangladesh: As per the the report, “A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities,” extreme heat cost our nation $18 billion in lost labour productivity and wiped out 465,000 jobs in Dhaka alone in 2024. That this is projected to double in about 50 years is a reality we must prepare for from today itself, and do all we can to ensure that the worst does not come to pass. What is most distressing about this is that it is hitting the poorest workers the hardest, thereby contributing to our widening inequality and undermining our development trajectory. Our cities, especially Dhaka, have been trapped in a dangerous cycle of rising temperatures, expanding concrete, shrinking green spaces, and worsening air quality. The result has been all too predictable, with workers unable to continue or facing unbearable conditions to continue working. To say Bangladesh must build heat‑resilient towns and cities is a gross understatement at this point. It is something we should have been planning for decades earlier. However, given the exponential damage extreme heat does to our nation on a yearly basis, it is time to begin redesigning urban spaces with shade, ventilation, and greenery, enforcing building codes that reduce heat absorption, expanding our tree cover in our cities, and enact major reforms such as rethinking our transport infrastructure. Better, more sustainable urban development is no longer optional but a survival strategy. Continuing to expand as a heat trap is not a solution, nor can it be classified as development. We must shift toward climate‑sensitive planning that prioritizes human health and economic resilience. Extreme heat is already costing billions and destroying livelihoods. Without urgent action, the losses will continue to grow. We must treat heat resilience as a national priority. Our future depends on it.

item.title: Poison on our plates. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-20

Food safety and environmental protection are inseparable pillars of sustainable development. A nation cannot claim genuine progress while its citizens are exposed to contaminated food and its natural environment continues to deteriorate. Unfortunately, Bangladesh faces serious challenges in both areas, demanding stronger governance, institutional accountability, and unwavering political commitment. Reports concerning food contamination have raised widespread public concern. Laboratory findings reportedly conducted by Professor Dr Abul Hossain of the Department of Chemistry, University of Dhaka, indicated elevated levels of chromium in broiler chicken meat, liver, brain, and commercial eggs. These findings have been attributed to the alleged use of chromium-contaminated tannery waste in poultry and fish feed, despite reported judicial restrictions on such practices. Concerns have also been expressed regarding arsenic and other hazardous substances in farmed fish. If confirmed through independent scientific investigation, such contamination poses a serious threat to public health and demands immediate regulatory action. When I joined the Bangladesh civil service, food adulteration was comparatively rare. Consumers generally had greater confidence in the quality of food, and ethical business practices were more widely respected. Today, however, food adulteration has become a significant public health concern. Yet this problem is neither inevitable nor impossible to solve. It requires honest leadership, effective law enforcement, public awareness, and accountability at every level. During my tenure as a Deputy Commissioner, I personally led campaigns against food adulteration, particularly during Ramadan, when the use of unauthorized colours and harmful chemical additives in iftar items was frequently reported. Regular mobile courts, market inspections, and coordinated enforcement by executive magistrates and law enforcement agencies significantly improved compliance. Although some business leaders initially questioned these measures, I asked one of them a simple question: “Would you like your own children to consume adulterated food?” His answer was an immediate “No.” That response reflected a universal truth -- every parent wants safe food for their family. Protecting public health should therefore unite, rather than divide, regulators and the business community. Bangladesh also needs stronger environmental governance. Over the years, substantial public resources and international assistance have been invested in forestry, biodiversity conservation, and climate adaptation projects. While many initiatives have contributed positively, questions have also been raised regarding the effectiveness and transparency of certain projects. Public investment should always be measured by tangible environmental outcomes -- such as increased forest cover, biodiversity conservation, pollution reduction, and climate resilience -- rather than by expenditure alone. Whenever credible allegations of irregularities arise, they should be investigated independently and impartially to strengthen public confidence. The same principle applies to institutions responsible for environmental regulation and food safety. Their success should be judged by measurable improvements in environmental quality and consumer protection, not merely by administrative reports or completed projects. Strong institutions require transparency, professional competence, and accountability. Although Bangladesh has enacted important legislation, including the Safe Food Act 2013, effective implementation remains the greatest challenge to its success. Regulatory agencies must strengthen laboratory testing, surveillance, market inspections, and enforcement across the entire food supply chain. Equally important, officials who fail to discharge their statutory responsibilities through negligence or wilful inaction should, where legally appropriate, be held accountable. Environmental crimes and deliberate food adulteration should not be treated as ordinary regulatory violations. They threaten human health, damage biodiversity, increase healthcare costs, and undermine sustainable development. Consideration should therefore be given to strengthening penalties for serious offences, ensuring swift prosecution, and enhancing judicial capacity to deal with crimes that endanger public health and the environment. Public awareness is equally essential. Governments, educational institutions, businesses, civil society, religious leaders, and the media all have a shared responsibility to promote a culture that values environmental stewardship and rejects food adulteration. Sustainable progress cannot be achieved through laws alone; it depends on ethics, integrity, and collective responsibility. Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to overcome major national challenges. There is every reason to believe that the country can also become a regional leader in food safety and environmental protection. Achieving this goal, however, requires a genuine policy of zero tolerance toward food adulteration and environmental crimes, supported by strong institutions, transparent governance, scientific evidence, and the consistent application of the rule of law. Protecting the environment and ensuring safe food are not merely administrative obligations -- they are moral responsibilities owed to every citizen. Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is a former Additional Secretary, Ministry of  Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Bangladesh.
